unit.subject: English
unit.unitOverview: Unit 7 explores point of view: who tells a story, and how that choice changes what a reader sees. Learners compare two first-person accounts of one market morning, then follow a Year 5 class in Ayensu who uncover a hidden mural and argue about what it means. Along the way they learn to separate facts from opinions, to use phrases such as I think that and In my opinion, and to agree or disagree politely with a reason. The unit ends with each learner retelling a familiar story through a brand-new narrator's eyes.
unit.learningPath: Preview the goals and the five word groups. Read Omar's account and Amal's account and compare them. Read The Forgotten Mural in three parts and answer the inference questions. Practise fact and opinion, opinion phrases, and polite disagreement. Plan, draft and revise a retelling from a new point of view. Perform the hot-seat, debate and dramatic reading, then complete the quiz and self-assessment.

readings.title: Two Voices from the Market: Omar's Account
readings.setting: Ayensu, a coastal town with a rural edge and a busy urban centre
readings.passageScript:
I have stood behind this stall since before sunrise, wiping the same wooden counter.
For nine days the fishing boats came back with nothing at all.
My customers walked straight past me without stopping.
My income dried up like a puddle in the midday sun.
I began to worry about paying my children's school fees.
Some evenings I sat at home and did the sums in my head.
My wife told me to be patient, because the sea always gives again.
Then, early this morning, I heard the rumble of the truck before I saw it.
I know that sound the way a mother knows her child's cry.
The big blue truck rolled slowly down the dusty road.
Silver fish glinted in the back, piled as high as treasure.
I shouted to the trader beside me, and the news raced through every lane.
People came hurrying from all directions with baskets grabbed in a rush.
I worked faster this morning than I have ever worked in my life.
I scooped ice from the cooler and laid the fish in neat rows.
I called out my prices as loudly as my voice would allow.
By midday my throat was hoarse, but I did not care at all.
Customer after customer pressed money into my hand.
My counter was sticky with scales and salt water, and my back ached.
Even so, I felt a deep relief and a quiet pride.
This is what it means to provide for your family.
I will never give up on this stall, however many empty days come.

readings.title: Two Voices from the Market: Amal's Account
readings.setting: Ayensu, a coastal town with a rural edge and a busy urban centre
readings.passageScript:
My mother woke me early and said we were going to the market.
I groaned, because the market has been so dull for weeks.
Every time we go, the stalls are half empty and the grown-ups talk about rice prices.
Today, though, something felt different as soon as we turned by the old clock tower.
There was noise everywhere, and people were laughing and calling across the street.
I could smell something strong and salty drifting through the warm air.
The whole street felt alive, like the morning of a festival.
My mother squeezed my hand and walked faster than usual.
We pushed through the crowd until we reached Omar's stall.
I have never seen so many fish in my life.
They were silver and blue and pink, and their eyes looked like tiny glass marbles.
Omar was shouting his prices so loudly that I covered my ears and laughed.
An orange cat crept from under the stall and tried to steal a fish tail.
Omar shooed it away with a rolled-up newspaper, and everybody around us laughed.
While my mother chose our fish, I wandered to the spice seller at the next stall.
She gave me a small handful of dried hibiscus petals for a sweet pink drink.
I held them carefully in my palm, afraid the breeze would carry them away.
On the walk home I skipped ahead of my mother and hummed a song from school.
The dull, empty street of last week was suddenly full of sound and colour.
I have decided that the market is my favourite place in the whole town.

readings.title: The Forgotten Mural, part 1
readings.setting: Ayensu, a coastal town with a rural edge and a busy urban centre
readings.passageScript:
In the rural town of Ayensu, the Year 5 class was given an unusual task.
Clay hills and riverbanks surround the town on every side.
Their teacher, Yasmin, stood in front of the board and tapped a map of Ghana.
“Today you are going to investigate a mystery from our town's historical past,” she said.
“There is an old building in the urban centre. It used to be the federal hall during colonial times. People say a hidden mural still stands behind a wooden wall.”
“A mural?” asked Amal, leaning forward.
“Yes,” said Teacher Yasmin. “A cultural painting. Perhaps a symbol of resistance, perhaps a symbol of peace. Your job is to find out.”
The next day the class travelled into the urban centre on a dusty blue bus.
Cars beeped and street vendors shouted.
The centre was loud and spacious, the opposite of their quiet village lanes.
At the hall a guard waved them through, and cracks ran across the stone walls.
Teacher Yasmin handed out journals. “Write everything down. Detect the clues like historians.”
Inside, cobwebs danced in the light.
Amal looked around slowly. “This place feels as if it is holding its breath.”
“Look,” said Sami, pointing. “There is a section of wood nailed over the stone.”
They gently removed the boards, and behind them was colour, faded but still alive.
A mural spread across the wall, full of people, drums and stars.
In the centre stood a child raising a woven basket.
On his tunic was a flag, half red and half green.
Around him, hands reached upward, and a lion watched from behind a tree.
“What does it mean?” whispered Amal.
“It must be local,” said Daniel. “Perhaps it comes from a festival.”
“It reminds me of our freedom day parade,” added Maya.

readings.title: The Forgotten Mural, part 2
readings.setting: Ayensu, a coastal town with a rural edge and a busy urban centre
readings.passageScript:
They took photographs and recorded everything they saw.
Sami drew a careful sketch and labelled each section.
Back at school the students held a meeting.
“We believe the mural shows pluralism,” said Daniel. “Different people, one shared hope.”
Amal stood up. “It could also show a peaceful revolutionary act. Something quiet, but powerful.”
The next week the class prepared a presentation.
They called it “The Forgotten Mural: Symbols, Space and Struggle”.
Maya began. “During the colonial era, many local stories were painted over or removed. We believe this mural was hidden on purpose.”
Daniel explained the flag on the tunic.
“It matches no real country, so it may stand for an early independence group. It is a revolutionary dream.”
Sami shared his drawing. “We added quotes from elders who saw the mural when they were children.”
They used prepositions carefully: at the back of the hall, during the early years.
After the presentation, Teacher Yasmin clapped warmly.
“You have done more than describe a picture. You have brought back a piece of forgotten memory.”
“But it is impractical to save the mural,” said one student. “The plaster is falling away.”
“True,” Teacher Yasmin agreed. “History does not need to be perfect. It needs to be remembered.”
Inspired, the class voted to paint a new mural on the school wall.
They divided into three teams: design, research and interviews.
Daniel collected stories from grandparents.
Amal found journal entries written by early community leaders.
One entry said, “We built with our hands and shared everything. That was our power.”
Maya asked the art teacher to help with colours.
“The mural will be big and spacious,” she said. “It will show rural and urban life side by side.”

readings.title: The Forgotten Mural, part 3
readings.setting: Ayensu, a coastal town with a rural edge and a busy urban centre
readings.passageScript:
They worked for two weeks, and every brushstroke felt like building a bridge between then and now.
One morning a visitor from the national heritage office arrived at the school.
“I heard about your project,” she said. “It is rare for students to detect meaning in symbols and then act on it.”
She looked at their sketches and notes. “Do you think this mural belongs to your school?”
“No,” said Amal. “It belongs to the whole continent. We are only sharing it, because it was lost for so long.”
The visitor nodded. “Your mural will appear in our heritage newsletter. It may even join the current youth history programme.”
On unveiling day, drums echoed from the gates.
Parents arrived in bright cloth and beads.
Elders stood beside the students, and the mural waited under a sheet of fabric.
“Today we celebrate memory,” said Teacher Yasmin. “A symbol can carry a whole story. Let us respect the voices that were once silenced.”
Maya stepped forward and pulled the fabric away.
Underneath was a thriving mural: dancers, farmers, teachers, city streets, a small flag and children carrying baskets.
A lion sat in the corner, exactly as in the original.
The crowd fell silent, and then the cheering broke out.
Later that week Sami wrote in his journal.
“Our mural is not just a painting. It is a statement. It shows what we value: pluralism, peace and courage. Political decisions are not only for royal or political leaders. They are for all of us, even students.”
Daniel added, “Symbols matter more than we think. A flag, a mural or a festival can bring people together.”
Amal finished the page. “We did not only find history. We made contact with it, and now it speaks through us.”

comprehension.question: In Omar's account, how many days did the fishing boats come back with nothing?
comprehension.correctAnswer: The fishing boats came back with nothing for nine days.
comprehension.explanation: Omar states the length of the empty spell directly in his second sentence.

comprehension.question: Omar says his income 'dried up like a puddle in the midday sun'. What does that comparison tell you?
comprehension.correctAnswer: It tells us his earnings shrank away almost completely, just as a puddle disappears in strong sunshine.
comprehension.explanation: The image links a vanishing puddle with money that stops arriving, so the comparison shows loss, not slow change.

comprehension.question: What does Amal notice about the eyes of the fish on Omar's stall?
comprehension.correctAnswer: Amal says the fish eyes looked like tiny glass marbles.
comprehension.explanation: Amal is close to the counter and describes what a child would look at first, so the eyes catch her attention.

comprehension.question: What did Teacher Yasmin ask her Year 5 class to investigate in the urban centre?
comprehension.correctAnswer: She asked them to investigate a hidden mural behind a wooden wall in the old federal hall.
comprehension.explanation: Teacher Yasmin names the building, its colonial past and the rumour of a painting behind boards.

comprehension.question: What did the class decide to do straight after Teacher Yasmin praised their presentation?
comprehension.correctAnswer: They voted to paint a new mural on their own school wall.
comprehension.explanation: The vote follows the praise and the news that saving the old mural was impractical.

comprehension.question: Omar ends by saying he will never give up the stall. What does that decision show about him?
comprehension.correctAnswer: It shows that providing for his family matters to him more than an easy working life.
comprehension.explanation: He lists aching feet, a hoarse voice and a sticky counter, then still calls the day a success.

comprehension.question: How does Amal feel on the walk home, and which detail in her account shows it?
comprehension.correctAnswer: She feels light and cheerful, because she skips ahead of her mother and hums a school song.
comprehension.explanation: Skipping and humming are actions, not stated feelings, so the reader infers her mood from behaviour.

comprehension.question: The class found the urban centre 'loud and spacious'. What does spacious suggest about the streets there?
comprehension.correctAnswer: It suggests the streets were wide and open, unlike the narrow lanes of their quiet village.
comprehension.explanation: The passage contrasts the centre with their village, so spacious is measured against what the children know.

comprehension.question: Daniel says the flag on the tunic may stand for an early independence group. What made him think so?
comprehension.correctAnswer: The flag matches no real country, so Daniel decided it must stand for a group's own dream.
comprehension.explanation: He reasons from an absence of evidence: no country owns those colours, so the flag is symbolic.

comprehension.question: What did the visitor from the national heritage office promise the students?
comprehension.correctAnswer: She promised that their mural would appear in the heritage newsletter.
comprehension.explanation: The visitor also mentions the current youth history programme as a further possibility.

comprehension.question: In his journal, Sami writes that political decisions are not only for leaders. What does he mean?
comprehension.correctAnswer: He means that ordinary people, including students, can shape decisions about their own community.
comprehension.explanation: The class changed how their town remembers itself, which is the evidence behind Sami's claim.

comprehension.question: Amal describes the spice seller giving her dried hibiscus petals. Why might Omar leave this out?
comprehension.correctAnswer: Omar was busy selling fish at his own stall, so he never saw the gift at the next stall.
comprehension.explanation: A narrator can only report what they notice, so each account keeps the details that mattered to that person.

grammar.title: Facts and Opinions: Telling Them Apart
grammar.explanation: A fact can be checked and proved with evidence. An opinion tells us what one person thinks or feels, so somebody else may reasonably disagree with it.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
A fact can be tested against evidence. An opinion reports a personal view.
Fact: The mural was painted on a wall in the old federal hall.
Opinion: I think that the mural is beautiful.
Fact: Ghana is a country in West Africa.
Opinion: I believe that Ghana holds the best festivals in the region.
The quick test: could a sensible person disagree? If yes, it is an opinion.
Judgement words are the clearest signal: best, worst, most exciting, beautiful, boring, should.
Facts often carry numbers, dates, places and names that can be checked.
Why it matters here: when you retell a story you constantly report what characters think, so you must know which of your sentences can be proved and which cannot.
grammar.commonMistake: Mistake: calling 'Ghana is a country in West Africa' an opinion because it appears in a discussion. Fix: ask whether evidence could settle it. A map settles this one, so it is a fact.
grammar.memoryTip: Hunt for judgement words. Best, worst, most exciting, beautiful and should nearly always mark an opinion.
grammar.practice:
Part A. Write F for fact or O for opinion. | The mural was found in an old hall. | I think that the mural is the most beautiful painting I have ever seen. | Ghana is a country in West Africa. | I believe that every school should have a mural. | The students prepared a presentation. | In my opinion, Amal is the bravest character. | Teacher Yasmin teaches the Year 5 class. | I feel that history lessons should include more art. | Part B. Sort these market statements into facts and opinions. | The market stands near the coast. | Omar sells fish at his stall. | The market is the best place in town. | Fish tastes better when it is very fresh. | The fishing boats returned empty for nine days. | Part C. Write one fact and one opinion about the new school mural, then underline the judgement word inside your opinion.

Answer key — Part A (in order): F, O, F, O, F, O, F, O. Part B: "The market stands near the coast" = F; "Omar sells fish at his stall" = F; "The market is the best place in town" = O; "Fish tastes better when it is very fresh" = O; "The fishing boats returned empty for nine days" = F. Part C is open-ended: check that your own fact could be tested with evidence (for example, "The mural covers the whole east wall of the school") and that your opinion contains a clear, underlined judgement word (for example, "I think the mural is the most beautiful artwork in town," underlining most beautiful).

grammar.title: Opinion and Belief Phrases
grammar.explanation: Opinion phrases warn your reader that a personal view is coming. Each phrase is followed by a clause, which is a group of words with its own subject and verb.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
I think that... shares an everyday opinion: I think that this story is exciting.
I believe that... shares a strong conviction: I believe that kindness changes the world.
In my opinion,... opens formally and takes a comma: In my opinion, the mural is a symbol of hope.
I feel that... shares a view shaped by emotion: I feel that the ending was surprising.
I consider... offers a thoughtful judgement: I consider this story to be very important.
It seems to me that... softens a claim: It seems to me that Omar cares deeply about his family.
From my point of view,... signals whose eyes you are using: From my point of view, the market scene shows how perspective shapes a story.
Structure: opinion phrase + that + subject + verb + the rest of your sentence.
Add a reason with because: I think that the mural shows pluralism because it holds many different people.
The word that is optional in speech after I think, I believe, I feel and It seems to me, but keep it in formal writing.
grammar.commonMistake: Mistake: writing 'In my opinion that the mural is important.' Fix: In my opinion takes a comma, never that, so write 'In my opinion, the mural is important.'
grammar.memoryTip: Say the phrase, say that, then say a whole sentence. If the words after that could stand alone, your clause is complete.
grammar.practice:
Part A. Fill each gap with a suitable opinion phrase. | __________ that Omar works very hard to support his family. | __________, Amal's account is more colourful because she notices playful details. | __________ that both narrators are telling the truth in their own way. | __________ that the market is a happier place when the fish truck arrives. | __________ that we should hear more than one side of a story. | Part B. Add a reason with because to each sentence you completed in Part A. | Part C. Write three sentences about the mural. Use a different opinion phrase in each one, and include one sentence that begins From my point of view.

Answer key — Part A (example answers; other opinion phrases that fit the pattern also work): 1. I believe that Omar works very hard to support his family. 2. In my opinion, Amal's account is more colourful because she notices playful details (this gap needs a comma-phrase such as In my opinion or From my point of view, not a that-phrase). 3. I think that both narrators are telling the truth in their own way. 4. I feel that the market is a happier place when the fish truck arrives. 5. I believe that we should hear more than one side of a story. Part B is open-ended: add your own reason with because to each sentence above — for example, "I believe that Omar works very hard to support his family because he takes on extra jobs at the market." Part C is open-ended: write three of your own sentences about the mural using three different opinion phrases, including one that begins From my point of view — for example, "From my point of view, the mural makes the school feel more welcoming."

grammar.title: Choosing Between 'Think', 'Believe' and 'Feel'
grammar.explanation: I think introduces an everyday view you might change later. I believe signals a deeper conviction, and I feel that introduces an opinion shaped by emotion.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
I think that the blue team will win the match. This is casual, and you might change your mind.
I believe that every child deserves a good education. This is a deeply held conviction.
I feel that the characters are brave. This is an opinion coloured by emotion.
I feel cold. This is a physical feeling, and it drops the word that.
Strength scale, weakest to strongest: It seems to me, I think, I feel, I believe.
Match the strength to the claim. A guess about a football score does not deserve I believe.
In a debate, save I believe for the point you would defend hardest.
grammar.commonMistake: Mistake: writing 'I feel that cold today.' Fix: physical feelings drop that, so write 'I feel cold today.' Keep that for opinions: 'I feel that the ending is sad.'
grammar.memoryTip: Picture think in your head, believe in your heart, and feel somewhere between the two.
grammar.practice:
Part A. Choose think or believe for each sentence, then explain your choice. | I __________ that it may rain before lunchtime. | I __________ that everybody deserves to be listened to. | I __________ that the red pencil is under the shelf. | I __________ that history should be taught in every school. | Part B. Decide whether each sentence reports an opinion or a physical feeling. | I feel that Omar deserved a good day. | I feel hungry after the long walk. | I feel that the poem is gentle and sad. | I feel warm beside the window. | Part C. Rewrite two sentences from Part A using a stronger or weaker phrase, and say what changed.

Answer key — Part A: 1. think (a casual guess about the weather); 2. believe (a deep conviction); 3. think (a casual guess about where something is); 4. believe (a deep conviction). Part B: 1. opinion; 2. physical feeling; 3. opinion; 4. physical feeling. Part C is open-ended: rewrite two of your Part A sentences using a stronger or weaker phrase from the scale (It seems to me, I think, I feel, I believe) and explain what changed — for example, changing "I think that it may rain before lunchtime" to "It seems to me that it may rain before lunchtime" makes the claim softer and less certain.

grammar.title: Agreeing and Disagreeing Politely
grammar.explanation: In a discussion you show respect by naming the other person's idea before you offer your own. A reason turns a bare reaction into a real contribution.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Agreeing: I agree with you because...
Agreeing: That is a good point. I also think that...
Agreeing: You are right. I believe the same thing.
Agreeing: I agree, and I would add that...
Disagreeing: I see your point, but I think that...
Disagreeing: I respect your opinion, but I disagree because...
Disagreeing: That is interesting; however, in my opinion...
Disagreeing: I understand what you mean, but I feel that...
The three-step pattern: name their idea, give your own view, then add your reason.
Saying only 'I disagree' sounds abrupt, because the other speaker learns nothing from it.
Changing your mind after a strong argument is a sign of good listening, not of weakness.
grammar.commonMistake: Mistake: replying with 'I disagree' and stopping there. Fix: acknowledge, disagree, explain: 'I see your point, but I think that the cat's version would be funnier, because animals notice different things.'
grammar.memoryTip: Climb the three-step ladder every time: their idea, my view, my reason.
grammar.practice:
Part A. Agree with each opinion and add a reason. | 'I think that stories are always better in the first person.' | 'In my opinion, adults notice more important details than children do.' | 'I believe that every story has only one correct point of view.' | Part B. Disagree politely with the same three opinions, beginning with an acknowledging phrase. | Part C. Hold a two-minute discussion about this statement: young people can change their own community. Use one agreeing phrase and one disagreeing phrase, and give a reason each time.

Answer key — Parts A and B are open-ended language practice: use the three-step pattern (name their idea, give your view, add a reason). Model agreeing response: "I agree with you that stories are always better in the first person because we get to hear the narrator's private thoughts." Model disagreeing response: "I see your point, but I think that adults do not always notice more important details than children, because children often spot small things adults overlook." Part C is a live, open-ended discussion — there is no single correct answer. Model self-check: a model agreeing example is "That is a good point. I also think that young people can change their community, because they often notice problems adults have stopped seeing"; a model disagreeing example is "I respect your opinion, but I disagree, because young people usually need adult support and resources to make lasting change."

grammar.title: Four Fixes for Weak Opinion Sentences
grammar.explanation: Four habits weaken opinion writing: dropping that, dressing a fact as an opinion, leaving out the reason, and mixing views with physical feelings.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Fix 1, the missing that. Weaker: I think the mural is important. Stronger: I think that the mural is important.
Fix 2, the fact in disguise. Wrong: I think that the sun rises in the east. Right: The sun rises in the east.
Right: I think that sunrises are the loveliest part of the day.
Fix 3, the missing reason. Weak: I think that the story is good. Strong: I think that the story is good because it teaches us about memory.
Fix 4, the muddled feeling. Opinion: I feel that the characters are brave. Physical: I feel cold.
Read your sentence aloud. If it stops before the word because, it usually needs more.
grammar.commonMistake: Mistake: writing 'I think that the sun rises in the east.' Fix: a checkable statement needs no opinion phrase, so write 'The sun rises in the east.'
grammar.memoryTip: Ask two questions before you write an opinion: does it need that, and does it carry a because?
grammar.practice:
Part A. Rewrite each sentence with the phrase in brackets. | The mural represents peace. (I think that...) | Students can change their community. (I believe that...) | The story has an important lesson. (In my opinion,...) | Everyone should learn about history. (I feel that...) | Art is a powerful way to communicate. (I believe that...) | Part B. Repair these weak sentences using the four fixes. | I think the ending is sad. | I believe that water boils at one hundred degrees. | In my opinion, the poem is good. | I feel that tired after the debate. | Part C. Rewrite each sentence with a different opinion phrase, keeping the meaning. | I think that the first version is better. | In my opinion, Amal is a very good observer. | It seems to me that Omar was worried about money. | I feel that the cat deserves its own version of the story.

Answer key — Part A: 1. I think that the mural represents peace. 2. I believe that students can change their community. 3. In my opinion, the story has an important lesson. 4. I feel that everyone should learn about history. 5. I believe that art is a powerful way to communicate. Part B: 1. I think that the ending is sad (Fix 1, add that). 2. Water boils at one hundred degrees (Fix 2, remove the opinion phrase because this is a checkable fact). 3. In my opinion, the poem is good because it uses gentle, vivid imagery (Fix 3, add a reason with because; the exact reason you choose is open-ended). 4. I feel tired after the debate (Fix 4, drop that because this is a physical feeling). Part C (example answers; any different opinion phrase that keeps the meaning is correct): 1. In my opinion, the first version is better. 2. I believe that Amal is a very good observer. 3. I think that Omar was worried about money. 4. I believe that the cat deserves its own version of the story.

grammar.title: Editing a Retelling for Viewpoint and Opinion
grammar.explanation: Editing means reading your retelling as a stranger would, then improving viewpoint, opinion language and punctuation one layer at a time.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Pass 1, viewpoint. Check that first-person pronouns stay the same person from start to finish.
Pass 2, knowledge. Delete anything your narrator could not have seen, heard or been told.
Pass 3, opinion language. Add at least one opinion phrase so the narrator's view comes through.
Pass 4, punctuation. Direct speech takes a comma before the closing quotation mark and a capital letter at the start.
Model: “The fish are here,” shouted Omar, waving both arms above the crates.
Split a paragraph whenever the time, the place or the speaker changes.
Read the final draft aloud. Your ear will catch what your eye slides over.
grammar.commonMistake: Mistake: letting a first-person narrator report a scene they never witnessed. Fix: cut the detail, or let another character tell the narrator about it inside the story.
grammar.memoryTip: Edit in four passes: viewpoint, then knowledge, then opinion language, then punctuation.
grammar.practice:
Part A. Find and repair the viewpoint slips in a partner's retelling. Mark every place where the narrator knows too much. | Part B. Punctuate these lines of direct speech correctly. | the fish are here shouted Omar | this place feels as if it is holding its breath whispered Amal | write everything down said Teacher Yasmin | Part C. Add one opinion phrase to each paragraph of your own retelling and a reason with because. | Part D. Write a two-sentence reflection naming one thing you found easy and one thing you found hard about writing from another point of view.

Answer key — Part A depends on the specific partner retelling you are editing, so there is no fixed answer: check that every detail could be known by the narrator, and cut or rephrase anything the narrator could not have seen, heard or been told. Part B: 1. "The fish are here," shouted Omar. 2. "This place feels as if it is holding its breath," whispered Amal. 3. "Write everything down," said Teacher Yasmin. Parts C and D are open-ended, based on your own retelling and reflection: a model Part C addition is "I think that Omar's worry shows how much he loves his family, because he never stops working"; a model Part D reflection is "I found adding punctuation to speech easy, but I found it hard to remember what my narrator could not have known."

speaking.title: Speaking 1: Hot-Seating a Narrator
speaking.instructionsAndModelLines:
One person sits in the hot seat and answers as a character from this unit.
Choose from Omar, Amal, the spice seller, the orange cat, Teacher Yasmin, Sami, Daniel or Maya.
The group asks questions, and the volunteer replies in character using I, me and my.
Model questions: How did you feel when the truck rolled down the road?
Model questions: What did you notice first when the boards came away from the wall?
Model questions: What were you doing on the day before the fish arrived?
Model answer as Omar: I felt my heart lift, because nine empty days had nearly closed my stall.
Model answer as Amal: I wanted to keep the orange cat, but my mother pulled me back.
Swap after five minutes so a new character takes the seat, then compare what changed.
Working at home, a family member can ask the questions, or your tutor can interview you.
speaking.aiTutorPrompt: Interview me as one character from Unit 7 while an adult listens, and tell me whether I stayed inside that character's knowledge.

speaking.title: Speaking 2: Opinion Debate
speaking.instructionsAndModelLines:
A debate is a structured discussion in which two teams argue for and against one statement.
Choose a topic: stories are always better when a child narrates them.
Choose a topic: hearing the hero's point of view matters more than hearing the villain's.
Choose a topic: everyone in a story has the right to tell their own version of events.
Choose a topic: changing the point of view of a famous story always changes its message.
Divide into a For team and an Against team, and give each speaker one minute.
Every speaker must open with an opinion phrase and close with a reason.
Model line: In my opinion, a child narrator notices more colour, because a child is not counting money.
Begin every disagreement with an acknowledging phrase such as I see your point, but...
The audience votes at the end, and the group discusses who changed their mind and why.
speaking.aiTutorPrompt: Take the opposite side of one Unit 7 debate topic with me while an adult supervises, and check that I gave a reason every time.

speaking.title: Speaking 3: Retelling Race
speaking.instructionsAndModelLines:
This is a fast game that shows how quickly you can switch between points of view.
One person reads a short passage aloud, using Omar's account or Amal's account.
The listener then retells the same events as a different character, in exactly one minute.
Start the timer the moment the reteller begins to speak.
Model opening as the orange cat: I smelled the silver fish long before the people did.
The group scores three things: accuracy, creativity and fluency, out of four marks each.
Accuracy means the main events survive; creativity means the new details fit the character.
Working alone, record yourself and listen back for moments when you slipped out of character.
speaking.aiTutorPrompt: Time a one-minute retelling with me while an adult is present, then tell me which details did not fit my chosen narrator.

speaking.title: Speaking 4: Dramatic Reading of Two Voices
speaking.instructionsAndModelLines:
Two speakers read the market accounts aloud, one after the other, to an audience.
The aim is to bring each narrator to life through the voice alone, without acting it out.
Read your version silently twice first, so you can lift your eyes from the page.
Omar sounds serious, tired and then deeply relieved; Amal sounds curious, playful and quick.
Slow down for thoughtful lines, speed up for busy lines, and pause before an important sentence.
Model delivery: pause after 'nine days', then let the truck sentence run faster.
Change your voice slightly for words spoken inside the passage, such as Omar calling out prices.
Afterwards the audience discusses which reading felt more emotional and which was more fun.
speaking.aiTutorPrompt: Listen to my dramatic reading with an adult nearby and comment on my pace, my pauses and how well my voice matched the narrator.

speaking.title: Speaking 5: Vocabulary Expert Interview
speaking.origin: Ehel English Content Template v1.2 curriculum expansion
speaking.instructionsAndModelLines:
Choose six words from this unit, including at least one from the Story Words group.
Your partner interviews you as the class expert on those six words.
For each word give the meaning, a full example sentence and a link to the unit texts.
Model answer: A synopsis is a short summary of a story, and I wrote one for the mural story.
Model answer: Pluralism means different groups living together well, which is what Daniel saw in the mural.
Your partner then asks one follow-up question about each word.
Swap roles so both speakers explain a different set of six words.
speaking.aiTutorPrompt: Interview me as the class expert on six Unit 7 words while an adult listens, and correct any meaning I explain loosely.

speaking.title: Speaking 6: Explain, Respond and Reconsider
speaking.origin: Ehel English Content Template v1.2 curriculum expansion
speaking.instructionsAndModelLines:
Explain one idea from this unit in about thirty seconds, using a reason with because.
Suggested ideas: why the same morning produced two very different accounts.
Suggested ideas: why the class chose a new mural instead of repairing the old one.
Suggested ideas: why a symbol can hold more meaning than a paragraph of writing.
Your partner responds with an agreeing phrase or a polite disagreeing phrase, plus a reason.
Answer two follow-up questions, then say whether your view has shifted and why.
Model close: I still believe that the new mural was the better choice, because the plaster was falling.
speaking.aiTutorPrompt: Ask me two follow-up questions about one Unit 7 idea while an adult supervises, then ask whether my opinion changed and why.

writing.title: Writing 1: Retell a Story from a New Point of View
writing.promptAndInstructions:
Choose a story you know well and retell one part of it through a different character's eyes.
Ideas: a folk tale about a young shepherd, retold by the brother who feels guilty.
Ideas: a Cinderella-style tale such as Chinye or Settareh, retold by the stepsister.
Ideas: the Tortoise and the Hare, retold by the tortoise during the long, slow race.
Ideas: the market morning in this unit, retold by the orange cat or the spice seller.
Plan first with this frame: original story, original narrator, my new narrator.
Plan on: what my narrator knows, what my narrator cannot know, how they feel at the start, middle and end.
Plan on: two details I will add, and one detail I will cut because my narrator would not care.
Write two or three paragraphs, roughly one hundred and fifty to two hundred words, in the first person.
Check: first person throughout, only what your narrator can know, at least one opinion phrase, a clear beginning and ending.
writing.modelText: A strong response keeps one narrator's voice from first word to last, adds two details only that character would notice, and carries at least one opinion phrase with a reason.
writing.successCriteria: I answered the prompt; organised ideas into paragraphs; used precise Unit vocabulary; supported ideas with details or evidence; checked cohesion and punctuation; revised my work
writing.support: Plan topic sentences and supporting details, then use the word bank and a source model.
writing.extension: Vary sentence structures, compare ideas, improve transitions and strengthen the conclusion.

writing.title: Writing 2: A Three-Sentence Synopsis
writing.origin: Ehel English Content Template v1.2 curriculum expansion
writing.promptAndInstructions:
Write a synopsis of The Forgotten Mural in exactly three sentences.
Sentence one names the characters and the setting, sentence two names the problem, sentence three names how it ends.
Use no dialogue and no opinions, because a synopsis reports events only.

quizzes.question: Which word names a large picture painted straight onto a wall?
quizzes.explanation: A journal is a private notebook, a festival is a public event and a continent is a landmass, so only mural names wall art.

quizzes.question: What does the word 'rural' describe?
quizzes.options: Belonging to the countryside, not the city. | A time when one country controlled another country. | A large event with music, food and shared activities. | A book for private daily writing.
quizzes.correctAnswer: Belonging to the countryside, not the city.
quizzes.explanation: Rural describes countryside places. The other options define colonial, festival and journal.

quizzes.question: Choose the missing word from Omar's account: 'My ______ dried up like a puddle in the midday sun.'
quizzes.explanation: Omar is describing money that stopped arriving during the nine empty days, so income fits the sentence.

quizzes.question: Choose the missing word from The Forgotten Mural, part 1: 'The centre was loud and ______, the opposite of their quiet village lanes.'
quizzes.explanation: The urban centre is contrasted with narrow village lanes, so the missing word describes open, roomy streets.

quizzes.question: Which of these sentences is an opinion rather than a fact?
quizzes.options: Amal's account is far more exciting than Omar's. | The fishing boats returned empty for nine days. | Omar sells fish at a market stall. | The market stands near the coast.
quizzes.correctAnswer: Amal's account is far more exciting than Omar's.
quizzes.explanation: More exciting is a judgement that a reader could reasonably dispute. The other three can be checked against the texts.

quizzes.question: Which sentence uses an opinion phrase correctly?
quizzes.options: In my opinion that the mural should stay. | I think the that mural should stay. | I believe that the mural should stay. | I feel that cold about the mural.
quizzes.correctAnswer: I believe that the mural should stay.
quizzes.explanation: In my opinion takes a comma, that never follows the article, and I feel drops that before a physical feeling.

quizzes.question: Which reply disagrees politely and gives a reason?
quizzes.options: I disagree with everything you said. | I see your point, but I think that the cat would notice more, because animals watch food. | That is wrong and you know it. | No, the hero's view is the only one.
quizzes.correctAnswer: I see your point, but I think that the cat would notice more, because animals watch food.
quizzes.explanation: It names the other view, states its own view and supplies a reason. The other replies dismiss the speaker or omit a reason.

quizzes.question: A narrator who uses the words I, me and my is telling a story in which point of view?
quizzes.options: First person | Third person | Past tense | Direct speech
quizzes.explanation: First-person narration uses I, me and my. Third person uses he, she and they, while tense and direct speech describe other features.

quizzes.question: Choose the missing word from The Forgotten Mural, part 3: 'It belongs to the whole ______.'
quizzes.explanation: Amal is saying the mural belongs to far more than one school, so she names the whole landmass.

quizzes.question: Which word names the idea that many different groups can live together well?
quizzes.explanation: An invasion is a takeover by force, a synopsis is a summary and a surplus is a leftover amount.

teacherNotes.note: Model each opinion phrase aloud before learners write, and check the meaning of pluralism, colonial and revolutionary before independent work, since all three carry weight in the story. Accept spoken, drawn or written responses to the comparison table. An adult must be present whenever a learner records audio or works with the AI tutor, and no child should be left alone with the device. Give feedback on complete sentences, quoted evidence and precise vocabulary rather than on quantity.

Suggested tutor prompts for this unit, all to be used with an adult sitting alongside the learner. Ask the tutor to contrast first-person and third-person narration using one sentence written both ways. Ask it for five facts and five opinions about a market, then sort them and explain each decision. Ask it to suggest three details a chosen narrator would notice that the original narrator missed. Ask it to argue the opposite side of a Unit 7 debate topic and to insist on a reason each time. Ask it to quiz you on the thirty-three unit words, starting with the Story Words group. Ask it to check whether your agreeing and disagreeing sentences acknowledge the other speaker before they answer.

answerKey.answerOrGuidance: Places and spaces: local, urban, rural, spacious, continent, industrial. People, actions and events: detect, contact, conquer, banished, flee, nurtured, vowing, invasion, festival. Ideas and concepts: pluralism, symbol, cultural, political, colonial, historical, revolutionary, synopsis, current, surplus, impractical, royal, federal, mural, journal, foundling, plaintive, thriving. Accept mural in either the places or the ideas column if the learner explains the overlap.
The pairs are 1-b, 2-a, 3-d, 4-c and 5-e. Watch for learners who join detect to pluralism because both feel abstract; ask them to reread the definitions aloud.
Answers in order: rural, urban; journal; detect; symbol; continent; pluralism; impractical; colonial. Accept impractical only, not practical, in gap seven.

Facts are 1, 3, 6, 8 and 10. Opinions are 2, 4, 5, 7 and 9, with judgement words best, should, healthier, should and easier. Item 5 often causes debate; accept it as an opinion because nutrition claims are argued in the sentence, not proved.

answerKey.answerOrGuidance: Correct answer: mural. A journal is written in, a festival is attended and a continent is a landmass, so none of them can be painted on a wall.

Correct answer: income. Omar loses earnings, not goods, so surplus and invasion cannot fit; a journal cannot dry up.
Correct answer: spacious. The sentence contrasts the city centre with narrow lanes, so only a word about room and openness completes it.
Correct answer: Amal's account is far more exciting than Omar's. More exciting is a judgement; the other three statements can be checked against the passages.
Correct answer: I believe that the mural should stay. In my opinion needs a comma, that never follows the, and I feel takes no that before a physical feeling.
Correct answer: I see your point, but I think that the cat would notice more, because animals watch food. It acknowledges, states a view and gives a reason; the others do only one of the three.
Correct answer: First person. Remind learners that tense and direct speech are separate features, so past tense alone never identifies a viewpoint.
Correct answer: continent. Amal widens the ownership of the mural from a school to a landmass, so no smaller or unrelated noun works.
